title: Your Thumb Pinch Test Reveals the Truth About Your thumb tendons
description: Yesterday's pinch was endurance. This one is power: pinch-lift the heaviest thing you can off a table and hold it for three seconds. Your kilos reveal the truth about your thumb tendons - the strongest small cables in your body, and the least trained.

scenes.narration: Set a flat, pinchable object on a table - a thick book is perfect - and load it: more books on top, or a bag hanging from its edge, something whose weight you can increase in small steps. A liter of water is one kilo; use bottles to count. Now pinch the base object between one thumb and your fingers, lift the whole stack clear of the table, and hold it in the air for three full seconds. That weight counts. Add a little and try again. Your THUMB PINCH number is the heaviest load your weaker hand can lift and hold for three seconds. Write down the kilos. Keep them. The truth about the smallest strong thing you own is coming.

beats.title: COUNT WITH BOTTLES
lines: One liter of water = one kilo.

scenes.label: THE LINE FOR THUMB POWER
scenes.sub: under 3: thumb untrained - 3 to 5: building - over 7: industrial
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Five kilos pinched off a table and held is where a thumb stops being a digit and starts being equipment. Under three kilos, your thumb is untrained - not injured, not small-boned, simply never in its life asked to be the wall against a serious load, because almost nothing in a normal gym asks it. Between three and five, the machinery works and the increments come steadily, a bottle at a time. Over seven kilos held for three seconds, your pinch is industrial: the grip of men who handle sheet materials, ropes and tools barehanded all day. Put the number in perspective: you just lifted, with the side of one hand, what many people would not carry in a bag for long. And the thumb did the heavy half of it.

Here is the truth about your thumb tendons, in full. The thumb runs on a team most people never meet. At its base sits the thenar group - a mound of muscle that rotates and presses the thumb into your fingers' path. Down your forearm runs its long flexor, a private tendon in a private tunnel, one of the strongest small cables in the body. And at the thumb's base joint, a saddle-shaped joint found almost nowhere else lets the thumb oppose - the movement that makes a hand a hand instead of a paw. Your pinch lift grades that whole team at maximum. Clinicians will tell you the thumb carries roughly forty percent of hand function; lifters discover the same truth from the other side, the first time a pinch test grades their strongest-looking hand as ordinary. The thumb is not a helper. It is a co-author.

Now the surprise in your number: it probably did not match your crush. Men assume hand strength is one thing, a single reservoir every test draws from. It is not. Crush, support and pinch correlate loosely at best, because each loads different machinery in different geometry - and the thumb machinery is the least correlated of all, precisely because ordinary training never touches it. Your push-ups do not train it. Your hangs barely invite it. Even your crush work uses the thumb as a clamp, not a lifter. This is why a man can deadlift impressively and fail a five-kilo pinch: the reservoir model is wrong. Hands are committees. Your test today graded the committee member who never gets invited to meetings - and discovered he has been doing forty percent of the company's work, unthanked and untrained. The committee has a chairman, and it is worth naming him: the saddle joint at the thumb's base is what separates your hand from every animal paw and most tools. It lets the thumb swing across the palm to meet any finger, which is why your pinch can be aimed, not just squeezed. When you train the pinch lift, you are training the most human movement your body owns. Treat it with the respect that deserves - clean angles, honest loads, no jerking.

One more link in the chain, one joint upstream: your wrist. Repeat your max pinch with your wrist bent forward and feel the lift die. The thumb's long tendon crosses the wrist, and like every cable around a corner, it loses force when the corner sharpens - and worse, it drags against the tunnel wall, which is why sloppy pinch training can make wrists grumble. The pros fix this without thinking: wrist straight or tipped very slightly back, forearm quiet, the thumb doing the talking. Check your own winning lift on video and you will likely find your wrist already knew this. The body protects its cables instinctively. Training is just making the instinct deliberate, then loading it on purpose, a bottle at a time.

The skinny advantage in pinch lifting is the fineness of your ladder. Your increments are bottles and paperbacks - a quarter kilo here, half a kilo there - which means you can live exactly at your thumb's current ceiling for weeks, nudging it upward in steps too small to fail. Heavy-handed training cannot do this; a strong man's pinch jumps in plates and gaps. And because the loads are small in absolute terms, your tendons recover fast enough for frequent sessions - the exact recipe cables respond to. There is a quiet satisfaction available here too: pinch strength is invisible in the mirror and undeniable in the hand. The first time you carry a heavy board one-handed by its edge past a man twice your size, this episode gets its thank-you.

We load the thumb together. Three rounds. Each round: pinch lifts at a weight just below your max, three clean seconds per lift, alternating hands, wrist straight. When a lift needs a wrestle, it is too heavy - drop a bottle and keep the quality.

Your week: pinch lifting on three days, built like a strength sport in miniature. Work up in bottles to a heavy-but-clean triple of three-second holds per hand, then stop - max pinch work is tendon work, and tendons like their heavy days spaced, with the moderate days from the pinch hold episode in between. Two errors to refuse. Jerking the load off the table, which borrows momentum your thumb did not make and teaches the tendons nothing. And letting the stack tilt so the fingers take over - the moment it tilts, the thumb has resigned and the lift is a lie. Flat, straight, three honest seconds, then down. Add a bottle when a full session passes without a failed hold. Patience is not the price of this training. Patience is the training.

scenes.label: WHAT YOUR PINCH LIFT MEANS
scenes.sub: under 3 kg: untrained - 3 to 5: building - over 5: equipped
scenes.narration: So what do your kilos mean? Under three, your thumb is untrained - a co-author who has never been given a chapter - and the chapters come fast once he is invited. Between three and five, you are building industrial equipment: the thenar team is learning to be a wall under real load, and your other grips are quietly profiting from the stronger partner. Over five kilos held clean, your thumb is equipped: a digit that changes what your whole hand can be trusted with, from boards to ropes to a partner's wrist in a scramble. Retest in thirty days, same setup, same three-second law. Comment your kilos below - and weigh honestly, because a guessed kilo is a rumor, not a result.

The strongest small thing you own just got its first honest grade. Whatever it was, it is about to climb, one bottle at a time. Thirty days of lifting with your thumb, then we weigh in again. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
